I'm a Process Automation engineer in the power industry! Oh I have so many answers, but how to keep it under 100000 words?

So in (more or less) any power facility, you have a fundamental reaction:

  • Fuel + Reactants ==> Junk + Energy

Your fuel can be just about anything - not important here. Just know that you're burning/reacting, whatever - releasing a lot of heat.

If you overheat, you cause problems. Hot gases, just leaving, can spit off free radicals and make NOx (ie, acid rain). You can also burn, scald, vaporize, melt, whatever.

You want to carry this heat to your turbines, not let it sit, overheat and destroy everything. Steam is your carrier - just moves energy from one spot to another.

What's the problem with fire? When it gets hot, it burns more stuff, and gets even hotter - burns EVEN FASTER. Of course this can get out of control quickly. Nuclear is MUCH, MUCH more dangerous in this sense than conventional fire.

Note the word control - we're going to use it in a technical sense soon.

Start simple:

  • Burn a unit of fuel
  • Get a unit of energy
  • User it on water to get a unit of steam
  • Unit of steam goes to the turbine
  • Turbine uses the steam to make a unit of power

I'm just using fuel-burn because it's likely familiar to you - fission & fusion work similarly enough for control purposes - they make heat.

Now we already have five steps - oversimplified. And we forgot some stuff:

  • We had to transfer some fuel & air into our fire
  • Can't just use magical "units"; everything has to be measured
  • Can't just have a campfire - we need a boiler/oven/something
  • What about the crap left over? Campfire smoke rises up & goes away, and ash can just be scattered or will wash away in the rain (hint: can't do that on an industrial scale)
  • How much steam do you need? What if you made too much?
  • I'm sure you've seen a leaky faucet before at grandma's house - what if you had 1000 faucets, some a hundred years old, and any leak in one could make somebody die?
  • What if your steam is leaking and you can't see it?
  • What if you make 1000 units of power, but the Power Company says you made 999? Who is "right"? What if you disagree?
  • What if your oven overheats? Ever read a recipe that says "oven temperatures may vary"? What does that mean?

Hint: your oven temperature can NOT vary. It HAS to be right.

It turns out that every one of those questions & problems is a control loop - or maybe a dozen.

You measure something (like temperature), and control it somehow (with a fan). And a computer.

You need flow rates. You have to weigh stuff. You need smart things to tell you if the computer is wrong or made a bad calculation.

See how complicated this is getting? We haven't even talked about what type of fuel we're using yet. I'll try to elaborate tomorrow - but I hopefully you can appreciate why so many things are important.
